analysis.one_liner: Lets landlords evict tenants immediately after the tenants file for bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee after its sponsor and 21 cosponsors signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: Under bankruptcy law, when someone files for bankruptcy an 'automatic stay' generally freezes collection actions, including evictions, while a court sorts out the debts. This bill would have made an exception: a landlord could keep evicting a tenant in bankruptcy without that freeze. It also would have kept the tenant's interest in an already-terminated rental out of the bankruptcy estate. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Landlords and rental property owners. Today, if a tenant files for bankruptcy, the landlord must ask the bankruptcy court for permission to proceed with an eviction — a step that takes time and gives the tenant a chance to object. The bill would remove that step, letting eviction cases proceed right away and ending any claim to a rental whose lease had already been terminated.

how_it_helps.text: It adds evictions to the list of actions the bankruptcy automatic stay does not block, so a landlord could carry an eviction case to judgment without first going to bankruptcy court for relief from the stay [S2] [S3].

It excludes from the bankruptcy estate any tenant interest in residential rental property whose rental had terminated before the bankruptcy was filed, so that interest could not be administered or protected as part of the bankruptcy [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tenants in bankruptcy. Filing for bankruptcy is one of the few moments a household in crisis gets legal breathing room; the bill would carve evictions out of that protection, so a renter who filed for bankruptcy could be put out of their home faster, with the bankruptcy court no longer standing between them and the eviction.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes a layer of court review: today a landlord must still ask the bankruptcy court for relief from the automatic stay before evicting a tenant who has filed, and the bill would end that requirement for eviction cases [S2].

The strongest good-faith argument for it is real: landlords can lose months of rent while a tenant in bankruptcy remains in a unit, and the stay can tie up an eviction even where the tenant had already defaulted before filing. The bill would have addressed that by letting eviction actions proceed [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The landlord's complaint — a bankruptcy filing can freeze an eviction and leave a unit occupied without payment — is genuine, but the bill addressed it with a broad exception rather than a targeted fix. The automatic stay is temporary and landlords can already obtain relief from it on request; this bill would have done away with that check entirely for evictions, at the expense of renters whose bankruptcy filing is often triggered by the same financial crisis that threatens their housing. The cost to tenants outweighs the procedural convenience for landlords.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee the same month, and nothing ever happened to it — no hearing, no vote, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Elton Gallegly introduced the bill on March 1, 1993, with five original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and two days later to the Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law [S1] [S5].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Renters facing bankruptcy are better off, because the bankruptcy protections they rely on to stop an eviction while their debts are sorted out remain intact. Landlords who wanted eviction cases to bypass the bankruptcy stay did not get that change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Renters in bankruptcy, whose eviction protections stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Elton Gallegly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt evictions from the bankruptcy automatic stay [S1] [S3].

against.name: Rep. Jack Brooks
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill after it was referred; it went no further than a subcommittee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was mostly Republican (18 of 21 cosponsors), but no votes were ever taken, so there is no record of how the chambers would have split.

industries.note: The bill would let eviction cases proceed without a bankruptcy court's permission once a tenant files for bankruptcy, and would strip tenant interests in already-terminated rentals out of the bankruptcy estate. The landlord's faster path to regaining the unit comes directly out of the tenant's protection during bankruptcy.
